q: Which of the following is an assumption of the kinetic theory of an ideal gas?
o: Collisions of the molecules with each other and with the walls are perfectly elastic
The molecules attract each other strongly
The molecules take up a large part of the container's volume
All the molecules move with the same speed
x: Kinetic theory assumes elastic collisions, negligible molecular volume, no forces except during collisions, and random motion with a spread of speeds. So only the elastic-collision statement is an assumption.

q: Hydrogen and oxygen are kept at the same temperature. The ratio of the average translational kinetic energy of a hydrogen molecule to that of an oxygen molecule is:
x: The average translational kinetic energy is (3/2)kT, which depends only on temperature, not on the mass of the molecule. So the ratio is 1; the factor 4 is the ratio of rms speeds, not of energies.

q: An ideal gas at a pressure of 1 × 10⁵ Pa fills a 2 litre container (1 litre = 10⁻³ m³). Using pV = ⅓Nm⟨c²⟩, what is the total translational kinetic energy of its molecules?
x: Total kinetic energy = ½Nm⟨c²⟩ = (3/2)pV = 1.5 × 1 × 10⁵ × 2 × 10⁻³ = 300 J. Stopping at pV gives 200 J; leaving the volume in litres gives 3 × 10⁵ J.

q: A gas occupies 3 litres at 27 °C and a pressure of 1 atm. It is heated to 127 °C and compressed to 2 litres. What is its new pressure?
x: p₂ = p₁V₁T₂/(V₂T₁) = 1 × 3 × 400/(2 × 300) = 2.0 atm. Check: compressing alone gives 1.5 atm, and heating from 300 K to 400 K multiplies this by 4/3. Using Celsius temperatures gives 7.1 atm.

q: Gas X has molar mass 4 g mol⁻¹ and gas Y has molar mass 16 g mol⁻¹. X is at 300 K. At what temperature do the molecules of Y have the same rms speed as those of X?
x: v(rms) = √(3RT/M), so equal speeds need T/M equal: T = 300 × 16/4 = 1200 K. Check: at 1200 K, Y has 4 times X's temperature and 4 times its molar mass, so √(T/M) is the same. Inverting the ratio gives 75 K.

q: Four gas molecules have speeds of 100, 500, 500 and 700 m s⁻¹. What is their root-mean-square speed?
x: Mean of squares = (1 + 25 + 25 + 49) × 10⁴/4 = 25 × 10⁴ m² s⁻², so v(rms) = 500 m s⁻¹. The ordinary mean speed is 1800/4 = 450 m s⁻¹, which is the tempting slip.

q: A rigid cylinder holds an ideal gas at 27 °C and 6 × 10⁵ Pa. Some gas is let out, and the gas left inside is then warmed to 127 °C, when its pressure is 4 × 10⁵ Pa. What fraction of the original mass of gas remains?
x: For fixed volume, n ∝ p/T: before 6 × 10⁵/300 = 2000, after 4 × 10⁵/400 = 1000, so half the gas remains. Ignoring the temperature change gives 2/3.

q: An ideal gas expands isothermally. The change in its internal energy is:
o: Equal to the work done by the gas
Equal to the heat it absorbs
Negative, because the gas does work
x: The internal energy of an ideal gas depends only on its temperature, which is constant in an isothermal process, so ΔU = 0. The heat absorbed equals the work done by the gas, but neither is the change in internal energy.

q: A gas absorbs 500 J of heat and does 200 J of work on its surroundings. The change in its internal energy is:
x: First law: ΔU = heat absorbed − work done by the gas = 500 − 200 = +300 J. Adding the two gives 700 J.

q: 200 J of work is done on a gas while it gives out 50 J of heat to its surroundings. The change in the internal energy of the gas is:
x: Energy gained = work done on the gas − heat lost = 200 − 50 = +150 J. Treating the heat lost as heat gained gives 250 J.

q: When a gas is compressed adiabatically, its temperature rises. The reason is that:
o: Heat flows into the gas from the surroundings
The gas does work on its surroundings
No heat leaves, so the work done on the gas all goes into its internal energy
x: In an adiabatic process Q = 0, so the work done on the gas equals the increase in internal energy, and for an ideal gas a larger internal energy means a higher temperature.

q: Air rushing out of a punctured tyre feels cool. The best explanation is that the air:
o: Gives its heat to the tyre rubber
Is compressed as it leaves the valve
Takes in heat from the surroundings as it expands
Expands almost adiabatically and does work using its own internal energy
x: The expansion is fast, so there is little time for heat exchange (nearly adiabatic). The gas does work pushing back the outside air, and with Q ≈ 0 this comes from its internal energy, so its temperature falls.

q: A gas absorbs 800 J of heat at a constant pressure of 1 × 10⁵ Pa and expands from 2 litres to 5 litres (1 litre = 10⁻³ m³). The increase in its internal energy is:
x: Work done by the gas = pΔV = 1 × 10⁵ × 3 × 10⁻³ = 300 J. ΔU = 800 − 300 = 500 J. Adding the work gives 1100 J; 300 J is only the work.

q: The internal energy of a fixed mass of an ideal gas depends only on its:
x: In an ideal gas there are no forces between molecules, so the internal energy is just the kinetic energy of the molecules, which depends only on temperature.

q: A gas is taken once round a complete cycle, and the net work done by the gas in the cycle is 300 J. The net heat absorbed by the gas in the cycle is:
x: After a full cycle the gas returns to its starting state, so ΔU = 0. By the first law the net heat absorbed equals the net work done by the gas, 300 J.

q: An ideal gas expands adiabatically and does 400 J of work. It is then heated at constant volume until it is back at its starting temperature. How much heat is needed?
x: Adiabatic: Q = 0, so ΔU = −400 J and the gas cools. To return to the starting temperature its internal energy must rise by 400 J; at constant volume no work is done, so Q = 400 J.

q: For an ideal gas, the molar specific heats at constant pressure and at constant volume are related by:
x: For one mole at constant pressure, the extra heat beyond the constant-volume case does work pΔV = RΔT, so Cp − Cv = R.

q: The molar specific heat of a gas at constant pressure is greater than at constant volume because, at constant pressure:
o: The molecules gain more kinetic energy per kelvin
Heat is lost through the walls
Part of the heat supplied does work as the gas expands
x: At constant volume all the heat raises the internal energy; at constant pressure the gas also expands and does work, so more heat is needed for the same rise in temperature.

q: 2 mol of a gas with molar specific heat at constant volume 20.8 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ is heated at constant pressure through 10 K. Taking R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹, the heat supplied is about:
x: Cp = Cv + R = 29.11 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹, so Q = nCpΔT = 2 × 29.11 × 10 ≈ 582 J. Check: 416 J raises U and nRΔT = 166 J is the work; 416 + 166 = 582 J. Using Cv gives 416 J.

q: For a monatomic ideal gas, Cv = 3R/2. Taking Cp − Cv = R, the ratio γ = Cp/Cv is:
x: Cp = 3R/2 + R = 5R/2, so γ = (5R/2)/(3R/2) = 5/3. The value 7/5 is for a diatomic gas.

q: An ideal gas with Cp = 3.5R is heated at constant pressure and absorbs 700 J of heat. How much work does the gas do?
x: Q = nCpΔT = 3.5nRΔT, and the work at constant pressure is W = pΔV = nRΔT = 700/3.5 = 200 J. Check: ΔU = nCvΔT = 2.5 × 200 = 500 J, and 500 + 200 = 700 J. 500 J is the rise in internal energy, not the work.

q: When a gas is heated at constant volume, the heat supplied:
o: All goes to increase its internal energy
All goes into work done by the gas
Is shared equally between work and internal energy
Is all lost to the surroundings
x: At constant volume ΔV = 0, so no work is done and Q = ΔU: all the heat raises the internal energy.

q: Nitrogen has molar mass 0.028 kg mol⁻¹. Taking R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹, the difference between its specific heats per kilogram, cp − cv, is about:
x: Per mole Cp − Cv = R; per kilogram divide by the molar mass: 8.31/0.028 ≈ 297 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹. Using 28 instead of 0.028 gives 0.297; multiplying by the molar mass gives 0.233.

q: A certain amount of heat raises the temperature of a monatomic ideal gas by 30 K when the volume is kept constant. For this gas Cp/Cv = 5/3. If the same heat is given at constant pressure, the temperature rises by:
x: Q = nCvΔT₁ = nCpΔT₂, so ΔT₂ = 30 × Cv/Cp = 30 × 3/5 = 18 K. It rises less, because part of the heat does work. Multiplying by 5/3 instead gives 50 K.

q: In each cycle, a heat engine:
o: Turns all the heat it takes from the source into work
Takes heat from the cold sink and gives it to the hot source
Does work without taking in any heat
Takes heat from a hot source, turns part of it into work and gives the rest to a cold sink
x: A heat engine works between two reservoirs: it absorbs Q₁ from the hot source, does work W, and rejects Q₂ = Q₁ − W to the cold sink. Turning all the heat into work is forbidden by the second law.

q: A Carnot engine of efficiency 40% absorbs 500 J of heat from its source in each cycle and completes 5 cycles per second. Its power output is:
x: Work per cycle = 0.40 × 500 = 200 J; with 5 cycles per second the power is 200 × 5 = 1000 W. 200 W is the work in one cycle; 1500 W is the heat rejected per second.

q: A Carnot engine could have an efficiency of 100% only if:
o: Its sink were at absolute zero, which cannot be reached
Its source and sink were at the same temperature
x: η = 1 − T₂/T₁ equals 1 only when T₂ = 0 K, which cannot be reached, so even an ideal engine cannot reach 100%. Equal temperatures give zero efficiency.

q: Two Carnot engines work in series: the first between 600 K and 400 K, and the second takes all the heat rejected by the first and works between 400 K and 300 K. The overall efficiency of the pair is:
x: Take 600 J from the source: engine 1 (η = 1/3) does 200 J and rejects 400 J; engine 2 (η = 1/4) does 100 J and rejects 300 J. Total work 300 J out of 600 J = 50%, the same as one Carnot engine from 600 K to 300 K. Adding 33% and 25% gives 58%.

q: A petrol engine has an efficiency of 25% and delivers a power of 15 kW. How much heat does it reject to the surroundings each second?
x: Heat input per second = 15/0.25 = 60 kJ; heat rejected = 60 − 15 = 45 kJ each second. 60 kJ is the heat taken in, not rejected.

q: A Carnot engine has an efficiency of 1/3. When its sink temperature is lowered by 50 K, with the source unchanged, its efficiency becomes 1/2. What is the source temperature?
Entropy is a measure of the:
o: Total heat contained in a system
x: Entropy measures the disorder (randomness) of a system; a change in it for a reversible process is ΔS = ΔQ/T. It is not the same as heat or temperature.

q: Hot water and cold water are mixed in an insulated vessel and reach a common temperature. The total entropy of the water:
o: Stays the same, because no heat leaves the vessel
x: Mixing is irreversible. The cold water gains heat at lower temperatures than those at which the hot water loses it, so the entropy gained (ΔQ/T) exceeds the entropy lost and the total increases.

q: An ideal gas in an insulated container expands freely into a vacuum. No heat enters and no work is done. The entropy of the gas:
o: Stays the same, because no heat enters
Increases, because the process is irreversible
x: A free expansion is irreversible: the gas spreads into a larger volume and becomes more disordered, so its entropy rises even though Q = 0. ΔS = Q/T applies only along a reversible path, which is the slip behind 'stays the same'.

q: Which of these processes is closest to being reversible?
o: Heat flowing from a hot cup of tea into a cool room
A very slow, frictionless compression of a gas, done in tiny steps
A gas rushing into a vacuum
A ball bouncing on the floor until it comes to rest
x: A reversible process passes through equilibrium states and can be run backwards with no lasting change, which needs a slow change with no friction. Heat flow across a temperature difference, free expansion and friction are all irreversible.

q: In each cycle a real engine takes 1200 J of heat from a reservoir at 600 K and rejects 900 J to a reservoir at 300 K. What is the total entropy change of the two reservoirs per cycle?
x: Hot reservoir: −1200/600 = −2 J K⁻¹; cold reservoir: +900/300 = +3 J K⁻¹; total +1 J K⁻¹. A positive total fits an irreversible engine (its efficiency 25% is below the Carnot value 50%). Adding the magnitudes gives 5 J K⁻¹.

q: An ideal gas expands isothermally and reversibly at 27 °C and does 900 J of work. The entropy change of the gas is:
x: Isothermal for an ideal gas: ΔU = 0, so the heat absorbed equals the work done, 900 J. ΔS = Q/T = 900/300 = +3 J K⁻¹. Using 27 instead of 300 K gives about 33 J K⁻¹.
